Rend. Sem. Mat. Univ. Padova, Vol. 137 (2017), 237–257
DOI 10.4171/RSMUP/137-14




            Coverings of commutators in profinite groups

               Cristina Acciarri () – Pavel Shumyatsky ()


Abstract – Let w be a group-word. Suppose that the set of all w -values in a profinite
   group G is contained in a union of countably many subgroups. It is natural to ask
   in what way the structure of the verbal subgroup w.G/ depends on the properties of
   the covering subgroups. The present article is a survey of recent results related to that
   question. In particular we survey results on finite and countable coverings of word-
   values (mostly commutators) by procyclic, abelian, nilpotent, and soluble subgroups,
   as well as subgroups with finiteness conditions. The last section of the paper is devoted
   to relation of the described results with Hall’s problem on conciseness of group-words.


Mathematics Subject Classification (2010). Primary: 20E18; Secondary: 20F14.

Keywords. Profinite groups, covering subgroups, commutators, verbal subgroups.

1. Introduction

A covering of a group G is a family ¹Si ºi 2I of subsets of G such that G D
S
  i 2I Si . When a group G is covered by finitely many subgroups, it is natural
to expect that some structural information about G can be deduced from the
properties of the covering subgroups. In the literature there are many results in
this direction. An important combinatorial tool for dealing with problems of that
kind is B.H. Neumann’s Lemma [29]: if ¹Si º is a finite covering of G by cosets of
subgroups, then G is actually covered by the cosets Si corresponding to subgroups
of finite index in G . In other words, we can get rid of the cosets of subgroups of
infinite index without losing the covering property.

    In recent years some “verbal” variations of the above questions became a
subject of research activity. Given a group-word w D w.x1 ; : : : ; xn /, we think
of it primarily as a function of n variables defined on any given group G .
We denote by w.G/ the verbal subgroup of G generated by the values of w . When
the set of all w -values in a group G is contained in a union of finitely many sub-
groups, it is natural to ask whether the structure of the verbal subgroup w.G/
depends on the properties of the covering subgroups.

    The questions become even more intriguing when the groups are profinite.
In that case the interplay of algebraic and topological considerations adds a new
quality to the obtained results. A profinite group is a topological group that is
isomorphic to an inverse limit of finite groups. The textbooks [32] and [42] pro-
vide a good introduction to the theory of profinite groups. In the context of profi-
nite groups all the usual concepts of group theory are interpreted topologically.
In particular, by a subgroup of a profinite group we mean a closed subgroup.
A subgroup is said to be generated by a set S if it is topologically generated by S .
Thus, the verbal subgroup w.G/ in a profinite group G is a minimal closed sub-
group containing the set of w -values. One important tool for dealing with the
“covering” problems in profinite groups is the classical Baire’s category theorem
(cf [19, p. 200]): If a locally compact Hausdorff space is a union of countably many
closed subsets, then at least one of the subsets has non-empty interior. It follows
that if a profinite group is covered by countably many subgroups, then at least one
of the subgroups is open. Thus, in the case of profinite groups we have tools to
deal with problems on countable coverings. Remark however that the Baire cate-
gory theorem does not provide a full countable analogue of the Neumann lemma.
A profinite group that is covered by countably many subgroups ¹Hi º is not neces-
sarily covered by open ones from the family ¹Hi º. For example, let Cp denotes the
cyclic group of prime order p and Zp the additive group of p -adic integers. Then
Cp  Zp is a profinite group covered by countably many procyclic subgroups but
of course Cp  Zp cannot be covered by open procyclic subgroups.

   The present article is a survey of recent results on finite and countable cover-
ings of word-values (mostly commutators) in profinite groups. Of course, finite
coverings of abstract groups are also mentioned here since in many cases they
serve as a starting point for the study of coverings in profinite groups. On the other
hand, it must be said that several important lines of research on the relationship
between Gw and w.G/ are not featured in this paper. In particular, the reader will
not find here any discussion of results on the verbal width (cf [34]) and problems
of Waring type (cf [23]).
                     Coverings of commutators in profinite groups                          239

    In Section 2 we describe known results and open problems on profinite groups
in which commutators are covered by countably many procyclic subgroups. Sec-
tion 3 is devoted to the case where the covering subgroups are abelian, nilpotent,
or soluble. Section 4 provides an account on coverings of word-values by sub-
groups with classical finiteness conditions – in particular by periodic subgroups,
or subgroups of finite rank. In the last section we discuss a recently discovered
phenomenon closely related to the famous Hall problem whether the verbal sub-
group w.G/ must be finite whenever the word w has only finitely many values in
a group G (the problem was solved in the negative by Ivanov [16]). We describe
results showing that in some cases w.G/ must be finite whenever the word w has
only countably many values in a profinite group G . The paper contains many open
problems and conjectures related to the topic of covering of word-values by sub-
groups.
    We thank the unknown referee for a number of useful suggestions on the earlier
version of the article.


Notation

Given a profinite group G , we denote by .G/ the set of prime divisors of the
orders of finite continuous homomorphic images of G . We say that G is a  -group
if .G/   and G is a  0 -group if .G/ \  D ;. If m is an integer, then we
denote by .m/ the set of prime divisors of m. If  is a set of primes, we denote by
O .G/ the maximal normal  -subgroup of G and by O 0 .G/ the maximal normal
 0 -subgroup.
     As usual, the expression “.a; b; c; : : :/-bounded” means “bounded from above
by some function which depends only on the parameters a; b; c; : : : .”
     A word w D w.x1 ; : : : ; xn / is said to be non-commutator if the sum of
exponents of at least one variable xi involved in w is non-zero. Given two arbitrary
elements x and y of a group G , their commutator is defined as the element Œx; y D
x 1 y 1 xy . The verbal subgroup of G corresponding to the word Œx1 ; x2  is the
commutator subgroup G 0 . The lower central words k , are defined recursively by

              1 D x1 ;      k D Œ k 1 ; xk  D Œx1 ; : : : ; xk ;    for k  2.

The corresponding verbal subgroups k .G/ are the terms of the lower central
series of G . Another family of words that generalize the simple commutator is
that of the derived words ık , on 2k variables, which are defined recursively by

  ı0 D x1 ;   ık D Œık 1 .x1 ; : : : ; x2k 1 /; ık 1 .x2k 1 C1 ; : : : ; x2k /;   for k  1.

The verbal subgroup that corresponds to the word ık is the familiar k th derived
subgroup of G usually denoted by G .k/ .
    Many results described in this article deal with so called multilinear commuta-
tors, also known under the name of outer commutator words. These are the words
that have a form of a multilinear Lie monomial, i.e., the words that are constructed
by nesting commutators. The number of indeterminates used in the expression of
a multilinear commutator word w is called the weight of w . For instance the word
                               ŒŒx1 ; x2 ; Œy1 ; y2 ; y3 ; z

is a multilinear commutator of weight six. Other examples of multilinear commu-
tators are provided by the aforementioned lower central words k of weight k and
derived words ık of weight 2k . The Engel word Œx1 ; x2 ; x2 ; x2  is an example of a
commutator word which is not a multilinear commutator.

2. Coverings by procyclic subgroups

On groups covered by few cyclic subgroups

It was pointed out by Baer (cf [33, p. 105]) that an abstract group covered by finitely
many cyclic subgroups is either cyclic or finite. Somewhat surprizingly, it seems
that until recently there was no published work on finite groups covered by few
cyclic subgroups. That gap was filled in [3]. In particular, the article [3] contains
the following results.
    1. Let G be a finite noncyclic p -group covered by m cyclic subgroups. Then
the order of G is m-bounded.
    2. Let G be a finite group covered by m cyclic subgroups. Then G has a normal
subgroup M of m-bounded order with the property that G=M is cyclic.
    Combining the above results it is not difficult to deduce the following theorem.

   Theorem 2.1. If a finite group G is covered by m cyclic subgroups, then G is
a product of a normal subgroup M of m-bounded order and a cyclic subgroup H
such that .jM j; jH j/ D 1. Conversely, assume that a finite group G is a product of
a normal subgroup M and a cyclic subgroup H such that .jM j; jH j/ D 1. Then
G is covered by jM j-boundedly many cyclic subgroups.

   Sketch of the proof.. Let m  1 and assume that G is a finite group covered
by m cyclic subgroups. Let us show that G is a product of a normal subgroup M
of m-bounded order and a cyclic subgroup H such that .jM j; jH j/ D 1.
   Let K be the maximum of orders of noncyclic Sylow p -subgroups of G .
We know that K is bounded in terms of m only. Further, G has a normal subgroup

N of m-bounded order with the property that G=N is cyclic. Without loss of
generality we assume that N ¤ 1. Denote by  the set of all primes for which
the order of a Sylow p -subgroup of G is at least KjN jŒG W CG .N /. It follows
that for any p 2  the Sylow p -subgroup P of G is cyclic and has the property
that P \ N  Z.N /. Let N1 be the subgroup generated by all Sylow p -subgroups
of N , where p 2  . It follows that N1  Z.N / and N1 D O .N /. Therefore
N D N1  N2 , where N2 D O 0 .N /.
    Suppose now that N is actually a p -group for some p 2  . Let P be the
Sylow p -subgroup of G . It is clear that P is normal. We will now use the fact
that whenever T is a cyclic p -group and ˛ a p 0 -automorphism of T we either
have T D ŒT; ˛ or ˛ D 1. It follows that in our situation either P  G 0 or
P  Z.G/. The former inclusion is impossible since jG 0 j  jN j while jP j > jN j.
Thus P  Z.G/. It follows that G is nilpotent. Since G 0  P and P is cyclic, we
conclude that G is actually abelian.
    Thus, we showed that if N is a p -group for some p 2  , then G is abelian.
Applying this argument to G=Op0 .N / for each p 2  we conclude that G 0  N2 .
Therefore all  0 -elements of G are contained in O 0 .G/. We set M D O 0 .G/.
It follows from the definition of  and the fact that G 0  M that the order of M is
m-bounded and G=M is a cyclic  -group. By the Schur–Zassenhaus theorem G
possesses a cyclic  -subgroup H such that G D MH .
   Now assume that G is a product of a normal subgroup M and a cyclic subgroup
H such that .jM j; jH j/ D 1. Let us show that G can be covered by m cyclic
subgroups for some jM j-bounded number m. Set  D .M / and denote by X1
the set of all  -elements in G , by X2 that of  0 -elements, and by X3 the set of
elements which are neither  - nor  0 -elements.
   It is clear that X1 D M and so this set is covered by at most jM j cyclic
subgroups.
   By the Schur–Zassenhaus theorem X2 is a union of (cyclic) Hall  0 -subgroups.
Since the Hall  0 -subgroups are conjugate, there are at most jM j of them and so
X2 is covered by at most jM j cyclic subgroups.
    Choose a generator a of H . Let n be the minimal number such that an 2 Z.G/.
Of course, n is bounded by jM j. Set Mi D CM .ai / for each i D 1; 2; : : : .

covered by at most jMi j cyclic subgroups. Each of these subgroups has at most

to a conjugate of a subgroup of the form hai ; Mi i. So the set X3 is covered by
jM j-boundedly many cyclic subgroups.                                          

On groups in which commutators are covered by few cyclic subgroups

In [9] Fernández-Alcober and Shumyatsky showed that if G is an abstract group
in which the set of all commutators is covered by finitely many cyclic subgroups,
then the commutator subgroup G 0 either is finite or cyclic. Further information on
the structure of such groups was obtained in [11] where the following result was
proved.

   Theorem 2.2. Let G be a group that possesses m cyclic subgroups whose
union contains all commutators of G . Then G has a characteristic subgroup M
contained in G 0 such that the order of M is m-bounded and G 0 =M is cyclic.

   Of course, the above theorem is meaningful only in the case where G 0 is finite,
since otherwise G 0 is cyclic. Comparing Theorem 2.2 with Theorem 2.1 it is
natural to wonder whether further details on the structure of G 0 in Theorem 2.2
can be obtained.

   Problem 2.3. Let G be a group that possesses m cyclic subgroups whose union
contains all commutators of G and suppose that G 0 is finite. Is G 0 a product of
a normal subgroup M of m-bounded order and a cyclic subgroup H such that
.jM j; jH j/ D 1?

Further results on coverings by few cyclic subgroups

The above results suggest questions on the structure of a group in which the set
of all w -values is covered by finitely many cyclic subgroups. In [6] Cutolo and
Nicotera showed that if w is a non-commutator word and G is an abstract group
in which the set of all w -values is covered by finitely many cyclic subgroups, then
w.G/ is finite-by-cyclic. Further, they showed that if the set of all k -commutators
in G is covered by finitely many cyclic subgroups, then k .G/ is finite-by-cyclic.
They also showed that k .G/ can be both noncyclic and infinite. It seems rea-
sonable to expect that the structure of k .G/ depends on the number of cyclic
subgroups covering the set of k -commutators.

    Problem 2.4. Let k be a positive integer and G a group that possesses m
cyclic subgroups whose union contains all k -commutators. Is k .G/ a product
of a normal subgroup M of m-bounded order and a cyclic subgroup H ?

    It is also natural to ask if the result in [6] can be extended to arbitrary multi-
linear commutators.
                     Coverings of commutators in profinite groups                 243

    Problem 2.5. Let w be a multilinear commutator word and G a group that
possesses finitely many cyclic subgroups whose union contains all w -values.
Is w.G/ finite-by-cyclic?

     It is clear that the above question has negative answer if we do not require
w to be a multilinear commutator word. The following example was given in [6].
Ivanov constructed in [16] a group K that admits a word v such that v has only one
nontrivial value in K while the subgroup v.K/ is infinite cyclic. Let G D K  K .
It is clear that v has only 3 nontrivial values in G and therefore the set of v -values
in G is covered by 3 cyclic subgroups. On the other hand, the verbal subgroup
v.G/ is not finite-by-cyclic.

On coprime commutators

The coprime commutators k and ık in a finite group were introduced in [35]. The
definition goes as follows.
     Every element of a finite group G is both a 1 -commutator and a ı0 -commu-
tator. Now let k  2 and let X be the set of all elements of G that are powers
of k 1 -commutators. An element g is a k -commutator if there exist a 2 X
and b 2 G such that g D Œa; b and .jaj; jbj/ D 1. For k  1 let Y be the set
of all elements of G that are powers of ık 1 -commutators. The element g is a
ık -commutator if there exist a; b 2 Y such that g D Œa; b and .jaj; jbj/ D 1.
One can easily see that if N is a normal subgroup of G and x an element whose
image in G=N is a k -commutator (respectively a ık -commutator), then there ex-
ists a k -commutator y in G (respectively a ık -commutator) such that x 2 yN .
The subgroups of G generated by all k -commutators and all ık -commutators are
denoted by k .G/ and ık .G/, respectively. It was shown in [35] that for every
k  2 the subgroup k .G/ is precisely the last term of the lower central series
of G (which is usually denoted by 1 .G/) while for every k  1 the subgroup
ık .G/ is precisely the last term of the lower central series of ık 1 .G/, that is,
ık .G/ D 1 .ık 1 .G//. In other terminology, k .G/ is precisely the nilpotent
residual and ık .G/ is precisely the k th term of the lower Fitting series of G .
     In the context of the above discussion the following results obtained in [3] are
very natural.

   Theorem 2.6. Let k be a positive integer and G a finite group that possesses
m cyclic subgroups whose union contains all k -commutators of G . Then k .G/
contains a subgroup M , of m-bounded order, which is normal in G and has the
property that k .G/=M is cyclic.
244                        C. Acciarri – P. Shumyatsky

    Theorem 2.7. Let k  2 and G be a finite group that has m cyclic sub-
groups whose union contains all ık -commutators of G . Then the order of ık .G/
is m-bounded.


On groups covered by countably many procyclic subgroups

Using the inverse limit argument the results on finite groups covered by few cyclic
subgroups can be easily extended to profinite groups covered by finitely many
procyclic subgroups. We therefore have

   Theorem 2.8. A profinite group G can be covered by finitely many procyclic
subgroups if and only if G is a product of a normal finite subgroup M and a
procyclic subgroup H such that .M / \ .H / D ;.

    This shows that Baer’s result that an abstract group covered by finitely many
cyclic subgroups is either cyclic or finite cannot be extended to profinite groups.
On the other hand, Theorem 2.8 implies that we have an analogue of Baer’s result
for pro-p groups: a pro-p group covered by finitely many procyclic subgroups
must be either procyclic or finite.
    The following theorem obtained in [5] describes profinite groups covered by
countably many procyclic subgroups.

   Theorem 2.9. A profinite group G can be covered by countably many procyclic
subgroups if and only if G is finite-by-procyclic.

   Thus, we have a pretty clear description of profinite groups covered by count-
ably many procyclic subgroups and we know when such a group is actually cov-
ered by only finitely many procyclic subgroups.


On groups in which commutators are covered by countably many procyclic sub-
groups

Profinite groups in which the set of commutators is covered by countably many
procyclic subgroups were studied in [5]. The groups were characterized as follows.

    Theorem 2.10. Let G be a profinite group. The set of all commutators of G
is contained in a union of countably many procyclic subgroups if and only if the
commutator subgroup G 0 is finite-by-procyclic.
                    Coverings of commutators in profinite groups                 245

    Specific questions on the structure of a profinite group in which the set of
commutators is covered by finitely many procyclic subgroups were addressed in
[11], where the following results were proved.

   Theorem 2.11. If G is a profinite group in which all commutators are covered
by m procyclic subgroups, then G possesses a finite characteristic subgroup M
contained in G 0 such that the order of M is m-bounded and G 0 =M is procyclic.

   Theorem 2.12. If G is a pro-p group in which all commutators are covered by
m procyclic subgroups, then G 0 is either finite of m-bounded order or procyclic.

    Several observations come to mind in the context of the above results. We
remark that in the case of pro-p groups there is a clear way to distinguish between
the groups in which the commutators are covered by finitely many procyclic
subgroups and those in which the covering requires infinitely many ones. This
is not so in the profinite case. Based on our previous experience, we make the
following conjecture.

    Conjecture 2.13. Let G be a profinite group whose commutator subgroup is
finite-by-procyclic. The commutators in G are covered by finitely many procyclic
subgroups if and only if G 0 is a product of a normal finite subgroup M and a
procyclic subgroup H such that .M / \ .H / D ;.

    A noteworthy fact that can be easily deduced from Theorem 2.10 is that if the
set of commutators in a pro-p group G is contained in a union of countably many
procyclic subgroups of G 0 , then at least one of the subgroups is open in G 0 .
    Finally, we remark that if the set of commutators in a profinite group G is
contained in a union of countably many procyclic subgroups, then the entire com-
mutator subgroup G 0 admits a covering by countably many procyclic subgroups.
This follows from Theorems 2.10 and 2.9. But of course we cannot claim that the
family of procyclic subgroups that covers the set of all commutators is necessarily
the same as the one that covers G 0 .

3. Coverings by abelian, nilpotent, and soluble subgroups

On groups covered by few nilpotent subgroups

Suppose that a group G is covered by finitely many abelian subgroups. In view
of Neumann’s lemma we can assume that each of the subgroups has finite index.
Therefore their intersection has finite index, too. It is clear that the intersection
246                         C. Acciarri – P. Shumyatsky

lies in the center of G and therefore the group G is central-by-finite. On the other
hand, any group G is covered by the abelian subgroups of the form hg; Z.G/i,
where g 2 G . Therefore if the center Z.G/ has finite index in G , then G is covered
by finitely many abelian subgroups. Thus, a group G admits a finite covering by
abelian subgroups if and only if G is central-by-finite. This observation is due to
Baer (cf [33, 4.16]).
    Let Zi .G/ denote the i th term of the upper central series of G . It is easy to
check that the subgroup hg; Zi .G/i is nilpotent of class at most i for any g 2 G .
Therefore any group for which there exists m such that Zm .G/ has finite index is
covered by finitely many nilpotent subgroups. In 1992 M. J. Tomkinson proved the
converse: if a group G admits a finite covering by nilpotent subgroups, then there
exists some positive integer m such that Zm .G/ has finite index in G [39]. In view
of Hall’s theorem [14] it follows that a group G has a finite covering by nilpotent
subgroups if and only if G is finite-by-nilpotent.
    The above results apply to both abstract and profinite groups. Recently it was
discovered that in the case of profinite groups similar results hold even with finite
coverings replaced by countable ones. The following theorems were established
in [36].

   Theorem 3.1. For a profinite group G the following conditions are equivalent.

(1) The group G is covered by countably many abelian subgroups.

(2) The group G has finite commutator subgroup.

(3) The group G is central-by-finite.

   Theorem 3.2. For a profinite group G the following conditions are equivalent.

(1) The group G is covered by countably many nilpotent subgroups.

(2) The group G is finite-by-nilpotent.

(3) There exists a positive integer m such that Zm .G/ is open in G .

    The proofs of Theorems 3.1 and 3.2 in [36] do not use the corresponding results
on finite coverings of abstract groups. As a consequence of Theorems 3.1 and 3.2
we can observe that a profinite group G admits a countable covering by abelian
(respectively, nilpotent) subgroups if and only if G admits a finite covering by
subgroups with the respective property.
                     Coverings of commutators in profinite groups                247

On groups in which commutators are covered by countably many nilpotent sub-
groups

Profinite groups that are covered by countably many nilpotent (or abelian) sub-
groups are understood reasonably well. Now it is time to have a look at groups
in which commutators are covered by countably many nilpotent subgroups. The
following theorem was obtained in [36].

   Theorem 3.3. Let G be a profinite group. The following conditions are equiv-
alent.
(1) The set of all commutators in G is covered by countably many nilpotent
    subgroups.
(2) The commutator subgroup G 0 is finite-by-nilpotent.
(3) There exists a positive integer m such that Zm .G 0 / is open in G 0 .

   Remark that no analogue of the above theorem for abstract groups is known.
Thus, the next problem is very natural.

   Problem 3.4. Let G be an abstract group in which the commutators are
contained in a union of finitely many nilpotent subgroups. Is G 0 finite-by-nilpotent?

   Actually, the particular case of the above problem for covering by abelian
subgroups was raised in [9]:

   Problem 3.5. Let G be an abstract group in which the commutators are
contained in a union of finitely many abelian subgroups. Is the second commutator
subgroup G 00 finite?

   Further, it is natural to ask whether in case of abelian subgroups Theorem 3.1
can be made more specific.

   Problem 3.6. Let G be a profinite group in which the commutators are covered
by countably many abelian subgroups. Is the second commutator subgroup G 00
necessarily finite?

   Finally, we formulate the related question for arbitrary multilinear commutator
words.

    Problem 3.7. Let w be a multilinear commutator word and G a profinite
group in which the w -values are covered by countably many nilpotent subgroups.
Is w.G/ finite-by-nilpotent?
248                          C. Acciarri – P. Shumyatsky

Coverings by soluble subgroups

Suppose a group G is covered by finitely many soluble subgroups. By Neumann’s
lemma G must be virtually soluble. On the other hand, suppose that G has a normal
soluble subgroup N of finite index. Then G is covered by finitely many soluble
subgroups of the form hN; gi, where g 2 G . Thus, G is covered by finitely many
soluble subgroups if and only if G is virtually soluble.
   The following result was obtained in [2].

   Theorem 3.8. Let w be a multilinear commutator word and G a profinite
group having countably many soluble subgroups whose union contains the set
of w -values. Then G is virtually soluble.

   A rather surprising fact that follows from Theorem 3.8 is that in a profinite
group the set of w -values is covered by countably many soluble subgroups if and
only if the whole group G is covered by finitely many soluble subgroups.

4. Coverings of commutators by torsion subgroups, or subgroups of finite
   rank

Coverings of commutators by torsion subgroups

A group is periodic (torsion) if each of its cyclic subgroups has finite order.
A group is called locally finite if each of its finitely generated subgroups is finite.
Periodic profinite groups have received a good deal of attention in the past. In
particular, using Wilson’s reduction theorem [41], Zelmanov has been able to
prove local finiteness of periodic compact groups [46]. Earlier Herfort showed
that there exist only finitely many primes dividing the orders of elements of a
periodic profinite group [15]. It follows that a periodic profinite group has a normal
series of finite length each of whose factors is either a locally finite pro-p group
or a Cartesian product of isomorphic finite simple groups. It is a long-standing
problem whether any periodic profinite group has finite exponent. Recall that a
group G has exponent e if x e D 1 for all x 2 G and e is the least positive integer
with that property.
    If a profinite group is covered by countably many periodic subgroups, by
Baire’s category theorem at least one of the subgroups is open and so the whole
group is periodic. In the present section we will look at the results that deal
with coverings of w -values by countably many periodic subgroups. The following
theorem was proved in [7].
                     Coverings of commutators in profinite groups                249

    Theorem 4.1. Let w be a multilinear commutator word and G a profinite
group that has countably many periodic subgroups whose union contains all
w -values in G . Then w.G/ is locally finite.

    Of course, under the hypotheses of Theorem 4.1 all w -values in G must have
finite order. Therefore Theorem 4.1 is related to the conjecture that if a profinite
group G admits a group-word v such that all v -values have finite order, then
the verbal subgroup v.G/ is locally finite (see special cases stated in [37, 22]
and similar problems 15.104 and 17.126 in the Kourovka Notebook [27]). This
conjecture is a natural generalization of the aforementioned Zelmanov’s theorem
on local finiteness of periodic profinite groups. Note that in this conjecture the
orders of v -values are not assumed to be bounded.
    Some particular cases of Theorem 4.1 were established in other articles. The
case of Theorem 4.1 where w D Œx; y was established in [2]. The case where
the set of w -values is covered by only finitely many periodic subgroups was
established in [1]. Since a solution to the problem whether any periodic profinite
group has finite exponent is not in sight, it is natural to study in some detail the
situation in which the set of w -values is covered by countably many subgroups of
finite exponent. A close inspection of the proof of Theorem 4.1 in [7] reveals that if
G is a profinite group that has countably many subgroups of finite exponent whose
union contains all w -values, then w.G/ has finite exponent as well. However the
proof in [7] provides no clue to the natural question whether the exponent of w.G/
depends on the exponents of covering subgroups.

    Problem 4.2. Let w be a multilinear commutator word and G a profinite group
in which all w -values are contained in a union of countably many subgroups of
finite exponent dividing e . Does w.G/ necessarily have an open subgroup of finite
exponent dividing e ?

   While finding appropriate techniques to handle the above problem remains
elusive, we do have quantitative results on the bounds for the exponent of w.G/.
The next theorem was proved in [1].

   Theorem 4.3. Let e; k; s be positive integers and G a profinite group that has
subgroups G1 ; G2 ; : : : ; Gs whose union contains all k -values in G . Suppose that
each of the subgroups G1 ; G2 ; : : : ; Gs has finite exponent dividing e . Then k .G/
has finite .e; k; s/-bounded exponent.

    The proof of Theorem 4.3 given in [1] is based on the Lie-theoretic techniques
that Zelmanov created in his solution of the restricted Burnside problem [44, 45].
250                           C. Acciarri – P. Shumyatsky

Theorem 4.3 naturally suggests the problem whether a similar result holds for any
multilinear commutator.

    Problem 4.4. Let e; k; s be positive integers and w a multilinear commu-
tator word of weight k . Suppose that G is a profinite group having subgroups
G1 ; G2 ; : : : ; Gs , each of finite exponent dividing e , whose union contains all w -val-
ues in G . Does w.G/ necessarily have finite .e; k; s/-bounded exponent?

Coverings of commutators by subgroups of finite rank

A profinite group is said to have finite rank r if each of its subgroups can be
generated by at most r elements. In the case of abstract groups the definition
is slightly different: an abstract group is said to have finite rank r if each of its
finitely generated subgroups can be generated by at most r elements. It follows
from results obtained independently by Guralnick [12] and Lucchini [26] that a
profinite group has finite rank if and only if there exists an integer r such that each
of its Sylow subgroups is of rank at most r . Pro-p groups of finite rank are now
fairly well understood – the theory of powerful pro-p groups [24, 25] provides the
techniques and methods for handling such groups. In the present subsection we
briefly survey results on coverings of commutators by subgroups of finite rank.
The reader will see that currently all known results are in parallel with the results
on coverings by periodic subgroups.

    Theorem 4.5. Let w be a multilinear commutator word and G a profinite
group that has countably many subgroups of finite rank whose union contains
all w -values in G . Then w.G/ has finite rank.

    Theorem 4.6. Let r; k; s be positive integers and G a profinite group that has
subgroups G1 ; G2 ; : : : ; Gs whose union contains all k -values in G . Suppose that
each of the subgroups G1 ; G2 ; : : : ; Gs has finite rank at most r . Then k .G/ has
finite .r; k; s/-bounded rank.

   Theorems 4.5 and 4.6 were proved in [7] and [1], respectfully. In the natural way
they suggest open problems analogous to the problems mentioned in the previous
subsection.

    Problem 4.7. Let w be a multilinear commutator word and G a profinite group
in which all w -values are contained in a union of countably many subgroups of
finite rank at most r . Does w.G/ necessarily have an open subgroup of finite rank
at most r ?
                     Coverings of commutators in profinite groups                   251

    Problem 4.8. Let r; k; s be positive integers and w a multilinear commu-
tator word of weight k . Suppose that G is a profinite group having subgroups
G1 ; G2 ; : : : ; Gs , each of finite rank at most r , whose union contains all w -values
in G . Does w.G/ necessarily have finite .r; k; s/-bounded rank?


Coverings of commutators by subgroups with finiteness conditions

Since the results on coverings of commutators by subgroups of finite rank are
similar to those on coverings of commutators by periodic subgroups, it is natural
to look for a common approach to both. First of all we remark that both properties
– being periodic and being of finite rank – are so called finiteness conditions,
that is, conditions automatically satisfied by all finite groups. Further scrutiny
reveals other properties common to all locally finite groups and groups of finite
rank playing important role in the context of our subject. It seems likely that the
above results are part of a more general phenomenon.
    Indeed, let † be a property of profinite groups such that
  1. every finite group is a †-group;

  2. the class of all †-groups is closed under taking subgroups, quotients and
     extensions;

  3. if a profinite group G is virtually soluble and G=Z.G/ is a †-group, then the
     commutator subgroup G 0 is a †-group as well.
   The following theorem was established in [1].

    Theorem 4.9. Let w be a multilinear commutator word and G a profinite
group that has finitely many †-subgroups whose union contains all w -values in
G . Then w.G/ has the property †.

    In the case where the coverings are finite both Theorem 4.1 and Theorem 4.5
can be deduced from Theorem 4.9. We do not know if Theorem 4.9 remains cor-
rect if the hypothesis that the covering is finite is replaced by a (seemingly weaker)
hypothesis that G has countably many †-subgroups covering all w -values. We
therefore state this as a conjecture.

   Conjecture 4.10. Let † be as above and w be a multilinear commutator
word and G a profinite group that has countably many †-subgroups whose union
contains all w -values in G . Then w.G/ necessarily has the property †.
252                              C. Acciarri – P. Shumyatsky

5. On conciseness of words in profinite groups

A group-word w is said to be concise if whenever the set of its values in a group G
is finite it always follows that the verbal subgroup w.G/ is finite. More generally,
a word w is said to be concise in a class of groups X if whenever the set of its
values in a group G 2 X is finite it always follows that w.G/ is finite. In 1957
P. Hall asked whether every word is concise and for a period of time this was an
open problem attracting interest of many group-theorists. In 1992 Ivanov proved
that this problem has a negative solution [16] (see also [31, p. 439]). On the other
hand, many relevant words are known to be concise.
    For instance, it is an easy observation by P. Hall that every non-commuta-
tor word is concise (see e.g. [33, Lemma 4.27]). It was shown in [43] that the
multilinear commutator words are concise (see also [10]). Merzlyakov showed
that every word is concise in the class of linear groups [28] while Turner-Smith
proved that every word is concise in the class of residually finite groups all of
whose quotients are again residually finite [40]. It was shown in [4] that if w is a
multilinear commutator word and n is a prime-power, then the word w n is concise
in the class of residually finite groups. In [13] the words Œ: : : Œx1n1 ; x2 n2 ; : : : ; xk nk
were shown to be concise in residually finite groups.
    There is an open problem, due to Jaikin-Zapirain [17], whether every word
is concise in the class of profinite groups. Of course, every word that is concise
in residually finite groups is also concise in profinite ones. An interesting phe-
nomenon was discovered in [8]. It suggests that perhaps the very definition of
conciseness in profinite groups should be relaxed.


   Conjecture 5.1. Assume that the word w has only countably many values in
a profinite group G . Then the verbal subgroup w.G/ is finite.


   It follows easily from [17, Theorem 1.3] that the above conjecture holds true
whenever G is a compact p -adic analytic group. The article [8] provides further
evidence in support of the conjecture. In particular, the results obtained in [8]
confirm the conjecture in the cases where w is a multilinear commutator, or
w D x 2 , or w D Œx 2 ; y.
    The proof of Conjecture 5.1 for the word w D ık is rather short (modulo some
results described in the previous section) and so we give it here. We require the
following simple lemma.
                       Coverings of commutators in profinite groups                       253

   Lemma 5.2. Let m  1 and k  0 be integers. There exists a number
t D t .m; k/ depending on m and k only, such that if G is an m-generated profinite
group, then every ık -commutator in elements of G 0 is a product of at most t
elements which are ıkC1 -commutators in elements of G .

     Proof. We use induction on k . Let H be the commutator subgroup of G .
As G is finitely generated, a theorem of Nikolov and Segal [30] tells us that every
element of H is a product of r commutators where r depends only on m. So for
k D 0 the result follows.
     Assume that k  1 and let u be a ık -commutator in elements of H . Write
u D Œh1 ; h2  where h1 ; h2 are ık 1 -commutators in elements of H . By induction,
h1 ; h2 are both product of at most t1 D t .m; k 1/ ık -commutators in elements of
G . Using the well-known commutator identities Œxy; z D Œx; zy Œy; z, Œx; yz D
Œx; z Œx; yz we can decompose u as a product of at most t12 commutators Œa; b
where a and b are ık -commutators in elements of G . The lemma follows.          

    Theorem 5.3. Let k be a nonnegative integer and G a profinite group with
only countably many ık -commutators. Then the k th commutator subgroup G .k/ is
finite.

    Proof. We use induction on k . Of course the result holds when k D 0 because
infinite profinite groups are uncountable.
    By assumption, all ık -values are covered by countably many procyclic sub-
groups. Thus, by Theorem 4.5, G .k/ has finite rank. If every ık -value has finite
order, then by Theorem 4.1, G .k/ is locally finite, and hence finite. So we now
assume that there exist elements a1 ; : : : ; a2k such that ık .a1 ; : : : ; a2k / has infinite
order. Without loss of generality we can assume that G D ha1 ; : : : ; a2k i.
    As G is finitely generated, by Lemma 5.2, every ık 1 -value of H D G 0
is a product of boundedly many ık -values in elements of G . Therefore H has
only countably many ık 1 -values and by induction H .k 1/ is finite. In particular
ık .a1 ; : : : ; a2k / has finite order, a contradiction.                                    

   Conjecture 5.1 seems rather hard to deal with. Even the case of the word
w D x p , where p is an odd prime, is unclear. Perhaps the next conjecture should
be more tractable.

   Conjecture 5.4. Assume that the word w has only countably many values in
a profinite group G . Then G satisfies a nontrivial group identity.
254                            C. Acciarri – P. Shumyatsky

   As a small step that eventually could be helpful in handling Conjectures 5.1
and 5.4 we will now show that under the above hypotheses the group G satisfies
a coset identity. Recall that a nontrivial word w D w.x1 ; : : : ; xn / is said to be a
coset identity of a profinite group G if there exists an open subgroup H  G and
cosets g1 H; : : : ; gn H such that w.g1 H; : : : ; gn H / D ¹1º.
   Thus, suppose that the word w D w.x1 ; : : : ; xn / has only countably many
values u1 ; u2 ; : : : in a profinite group G . For each i set
             Si D ¹.g1 ; : : : ; gn / 2 G      GI w.g1 ; : : : ; gn / D ui º:

The sets Si are closed in G      G and cover G      G . Therefore, by Baire
category theorem at least one of the sets Si has non-empty interior. It follows that
for some k the group G contains an open subgroup H and elements a1 ; : : : ; an
such that w.a1 H; : : : ; an H / D ¹uk º. Set
               v.x1 ; : : : ; x2n / D w.x1 ; : : : ; xn /w.xnC1 ; : : : ; x2n / 1 :

It follows that the word v.x1 ; : : : ; x2n / is a coset identity in G .
    We conclude this article by showing that Conjecture 5.4 is true when w D x p ,
where p is a prime. Indeed, we argue as above and conclude that for some k
the group G contains an open normal subgroup H and an element a such that
.ah/p D uk for all h 2 H . Let N D huk G i be the minimal normal subgroup of G
containing uk . By [8, Lemma 3.1], CG .uk / is open in G and therefore N is central-
by-finite. Hence, it is sufficient to show that G=N satisfies a nontrivial identity
and so we assume that uk D 1. If a 2 H , then H is of exponent p and the result
is immediate. Therefore we assume that a 62 H . It follows that H admits a split
automorphism of prime order p . Kegel proved that finite groups admitting such an
automorphism are nilpotent [18]. It follows that H is pronilpotent. If x; y 2 H , we
can find an a-invariant subgroup K  H containing both x and y and generated
by at most 2p elements. Khukhro’s theorem [20] (see also [21, Theorem 7.2.1])
tells us that K is nilpotent with class bounded by a function of p only. Of course,
this is sufficient to conclude that H satisfies a nontrivial identity and so does G .
